entry.evidence: into the climate system can cause temperature anomalies, precipitation irregularities, and floods

sequences.source_document: Liu et al. 2022, Geoscience Letters 9:13 (publisher XML text and PDF)

steps.action: Took from the literature the expectation that reduced solar activity lowers temperature, raises low cloud cover and alters precipitation, and so causes temperature anomalies, precipitation irregularities and floods.
steps.quote: into the climate system can cause temperature anomalies, precipitation irregularities, and floods

steps.action: Asked whether disasters from temperature anomalies, precipitation irregularities and floods in China differ between low and high solar activity periods, by location and season, over the last 2000 years.
steps.quote: the primary purpose of this paper is to investigate disasters related to temperature anomalies, precipitation irregularities, and floods

steps.action: Adopted the published dates of solar grand minima, inferred by other groups from East Asian sunspot records and 14C and 10Be proxies, plus the telescopic Maunder and Dalton minima.
steps.quote: data confirm that before 1600 CE there were 6 solar activity time-periods with relatively low solar activity

steps.action: Defined the minima as LSA periods and the intervals between them as HSA periods. Restricted the study to 1–1825 CE to avoid anthropogenic effects, and built an LSA-leading series and an HSA-leading series of eight cycles each (Table 1).
steps.quote: there are an 8-LSA-to-HSA (LSA-leading) cycle during 107-1794 and an 8 HSA-to-LSA (HSA-leading) cycle during 204-1825

steps.action: Extracted disaster items from the Song (1992) chronology of the 25 dynastic histories (6 temperature items, 4 precipitation items, floods in 9 river basins) and digitized them into annual 0/1 indicators with province or basin and lunar month (Fig. 1).
steps.quote: we convert qualitative historical records into quantitative data by marking years with disasters by “1” and those without by “0”

steps.action: Computed, for each item, subtotal and total, the proportion of disaster years in each LSA or HSA period, counting a year with several disasters once in the subtotals.
steps.quote: the proportion is the number of disaster years divided by the number of years in the study time period

steps.action: Ran a quick test comparing the 71-year Maunder Minimum with the other 1754 years: the ratios were 3.92 for temperature, 2.57 for precipitation and 2.51 for floods. This result motivated the full LSA/HSA study.
steps.quote: which allows us to quickly test if Maunder minimum results in a significantly high frequency of disasters comparing to the other study years

steps.action: Compared LSA and HSA proportions item by item in both cycle series: cold items and precipitation items are higher in LSA, hot items are higher in HSA, inland floods are higher in LSA and coastal floods are higher in HSA.
steps.quote: the proportions of disasters related to temperatures, precipitations, and floods are generally greater during the LSA period than those during the HSA period

steps.action: Applied Page's test across 19 disaster items to check whether the proportion of disaster years rises with cycle order. It does: T = 7.651 (HSA) and 8.050 (LSA), both above 1.645.
steps.quote: we employ Page’s test (Page 17) to see if the proportion of disaster years is increasing with the time period during HSA and LSA

steps.action: Attributed the trend to population growth and changing detectability in the historical books rather than to the hypothesis, and required that every LSA–HSA comparison be made in both the HSA-leading and the LSA-leading series.
steps.quote: This may be caused by the growth of the Chinese population (Lee et al. 13) and temporal changes in the detectability of disaster

steps.action: Built 90% confidence intervals for the LSA minus HSA difference in proportions (normal approximation, Agresti) for every item, subtotal and total in both series (Table 2). Intervals including zero were read as not significant.
steps.quote: 90% confidence intervals (CIs) for the differences between the proportions in the LSA and HSA periods are then constructed

steps.action: Checked agreement between the two series. The cold subtotal, the temperature total, the wet subtotal and the precipitation total are significant in both. The hot subtotal (HSA-leading) and severe drought (LSA-leading) are not significant in one series.
steps.quote: being significant in both LSA- and HSA-leading cycles confirms that the climate tends to be colder

steps.action: Refined the flood claim by location: inland basins flood more in LSA and coastal basins more in HSA (driven by the Southeast River Basin). The non-significant Taihu Lake result was explained by its near-coastal position.
steps.quote: In general, the inland and coastal floods tend to occur during the LSA and HSA periods, respectively.

steps.action: Split the 22 provinces into four areas (north/south of the Qinling–Huaihe Line, inland/coastal) and compared LSA and HSA proportions with 90% CIs (Fig. 5, Table 3).
steps.quote: The proportions of disasters are further examined in the northern inland, northern coastal, southern inland, and southern coastal areas.

steps.action: Concluded that significant differences are confined to the north, so the Qinling–Huaihe boundary matters. The HSA-tending southern coastal floods were attributed to the East Asian summer monsoon (cited).
steps.quote: This indicates that the climate boundary of the Qinling–Huaihe Line along at about 33°N could be important for severe weathers in China.

steps.action: Classified disasters by lunar-month season and compared the percentage of disaster years in each season between LSA and HSA (Fig. 6).
steps.quote: compute the percentage of the disaster in various seasons during LSA and HSA period

steps.action: Proposed from the shared Summer–Autumn concentration that irregular precipitation, mainly torrential rain, causes the floods, and that the solar effect overpowers the seasonal one. This was not tested further.
steps.quote: which suggests that the irregular precipitations most likely result in the floods

steps.action: Restricted the analysis to the telescopic era, 1645–1825 and 1645–1794 (Maunder, 8th HSA, Dalton), and recomputed the 90% CIs (Table 4). All three disaster classes remain significant.
steps.quote: The 90% CIs in Table 4 once again confirm that the disasters owing to anomalous temperatures, irregular precipitations, and floods occur significantly

steps.action: Kept the claim that China is colder, with more irregular precipitation, during low solar activity, and that inland and coastal floods favour LSA and HSA respectively.
steps.quote: the climate tends to be colder and experience more irregular precipitations during the low solar activity period

end.claim: In China during 1–1825 CE, disasters from cold temperature anomalies, irregular precipitation and floods were recorded more often in low than in high solar activity periods, with inland floods favouring LSA and coastal floods favouring HSA.

decisive_move.sentence: Without digitizing the Song (1992) chronology of the dynastic histories into annual 0/1 disaster indicators by item, location and month, there would be no proportions to compare between solar activity periods.

gates.evidence: The solar–climate expectation (§2 ¶1) directed which items were extracted and how periods were defined (§3 ¶1, ¶3). The underlying records were compiled long before, without this hypothesis (§3 ¶2). The 90% CIs could have included zero, and some did (§4 ¶8–¶9), but no physical rival was stated. Nothing was fixed in advance: the Maunder Minimum result was seen first and 'motivate the study' (§4 ¶1). The two-series design was justified after Page's test revealed a trend (§4 ¶5).

imports.item: Song (1992) chronicle of severe natural disasters and anomalies, compiled from the 25 official dynastic histories
Historical East Asian sunspot records and telescopic sunspot observations used to date solar minima
Normal-approximation confidence interval for a difference of two proportions (Agresti 1996)
Odds-ratio style comparison of proportions (Klotz and Johnson 1983)

limits: No 'first' or 'previously unknown' statement appears; Keypoint 1 (§1 ¶1) only says the records 'are converted into digital data and quantitatively examined'. The paper reports roughly 25 item-level 90% CIs per series with no correction for multiple comparisons. It does not address autocorrelation between years, which the CI formula treats as independent binomial trials (inference). No physical rival is considered, such as volcanic forcing, internal variability, or dynastic and administrative changes in record keeping. The only alternative addressed is the secular recording trend, and the two-series remedy is a design choice, not a correction of the trend (inference). Whether the solar-minimum dates were fixed before the disaster data were inspected is not stated; the Maunder Minimum result was seen before the full analysis. The text gives the cold-subtotal CI in the LSA-leading series as [0.015, 0.0057], whereas Table 2 gives 0.057. Table 3 appears to report only LSA-leading values, since its subtotals equal Series LH (inference). Sub-claims at other statuses: the Qinling–Huaihe Line as an essential boundary is best_explanation and untested. The claim that irregular precipitation or torrential rain causes the floods is a hypothesis resting on seasonal co-occurrence only. The East Asian summer monsoon explanation for HSA coastal floods is cited (Rao et al.) and untested. Hot-weather disasters favouring HSA reach regularity_in_range in only one series. The 'disaster and civilization as antonyms' remark (§6 ¶2) is a speculative extrapolation from Eddy (1976) and is not tested. No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded.
